doc.title: Putter Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 27, 2024

chapter: Bass function and the film role
title: Being in a movie, advice from Med Flory, and Sean Connery and Jill St. John
summary: Smith says he is not an actor but was in a film. He recalls Med Flory's advice about repeating hand actions, a rude actor, and working with Sean Connery and Jill St. John.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: You probably have run into people who think that you — when they find out that you play the bass they probably say, “Wow, you’re an actor and you also play the bass.”
Instead of the other way around.

Well I don’t run into that too much because where I play there are usually audiences, jazz audiences. And I have to say, because they say, “He’s also an actor.” “No, no, I’m not an actor. Alec Guinness is an actor. Meryl Streep is an actor, you know George Clooney is an actor. I’m a guy that was in a movie, but I never did anything special or anything, it was just a freak occurrence that put me in the movie and my wife says, “You’ve got to do it, you’ve got to do it.”
When you got on the set and got into that whole process, coming from a world —
You’re talking about the movie set?

Coming from a world in music where much of what you did was based and required improvisation, something different, was it a shock to you to do the takes over and over and it had to be the same way every time? Was it hard to adjust to that?

Well my wife was an actress and she was very, very good. And she was into, she never made any real money, she was in a couple of TV shows, but she — I used to help her with, she was improvising, and really very very good, when they had improvising theater. And so I used to, whenever she would have a part that she needed to study I would read, so I knew how to read a script. But now I’m starting — I went into a rearranged rap and I can’t remember what your question was. © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

Oh yeah, improvising. No I never thought of anything like that. It was just like I called around to different people and I said, “Gee I’m in this movie, what should I do?” And I called Med Flory and he was very, he was the only one that gave me good advice. He said, “Just remember they’re going to shoot the scene from different angles, just try to remember what your hands are doing when you’re saying certain things, and try to do it the same way. And that was the best advice I got. You know like, so after that I became aware of watching things and you see Burt Lancaster in an early movie where he’s eating with his fork and they cut away and they come back and instead of his fork in his right hand he’s got his spoon in his left hand. And you go oh, yeah, but that was a very good piece of advice from Med you know. And one of the actors I worked with I went the first day and I said, “Well you know I’ve never done this before, you know if you can give me any tips I’d appreciate it.” And he says, “Just shut up and stay in the background.” And I thought, “Well thank you very, very much, now I know exactly who you are.” You know and I’ve worked with plenty of people like you before and I know exactly, if I just stay completely — it actually gave me strength you know, knowing I was dealing with a jerk. But speaking of not-jerks, Sean Connery, wonderful guy, wonderful guy. And Jill St. John, wonderful chick. She was like a real musician’s kind of chick. And she had been married to Tom, what’s his name, I can’t remember his name, a singer that sings kind of like Frank Sinatra, a very good singer.

That’s right. Jack Jones, yeah Jack Jones. And she was lovely. She was lovely. But anyway, so it was, you know an experience not to be I don’t know if I did the right thing to do it but I did it. My wife said, “You’ve got to do it, you’ve got to do it. You’re not going to get another call like that.”
